questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The four subject matters of a lobbying contact
questions.learningObjective: identify the subject matters that make a communication a lobbying contact
questions.stem: The federal disclosure statute defines a lobbying contact as an oral or written communication to a covered official on behalf of a client about four listed subject matters. Which subject matter is one of the four?

options.text: The formulation, modification, or adoption of a federal rule, regulation, or executive order
The drafting of a state law that a client would like the national government to copy later on
options.misconception: believes state lawmaking falls inside the statutory definition

options.text: A request for a meeting that makes no attempt to influence the official at all
options.misconception: believes a bare request for a meeting is a lobbying contact

options.text: A communication made by a news organisation while it is gathering and disseminating news
options.misconception: believes ordinary reporting is a lobbying contact

questions.explanation: The definition reaches four matters: the formulation, modification, or adoption of federal legislation; of a federal rule, regulation, executive order, or other federal programme, policy, or position; of the administration or execution of a federal programme or policy, which includes contracts, grants, loans, permits, and licences; and of a nomination or confirmation to a Senate-confirmed post. Each is federal and each is about the exercise of national power, so a matter arising wholly in a state legislature is outside the list. The statute then removes a long set of communications, and among them a bare request for a meeting that does not attempt to influence, and the gathering and dissemination of news.
questions.hint: Look for the item that concerns federal legislation or federal programmes and decisions.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who the statute counts as a lobbyist
questions.learningObjective: state the two conditions in the statutory definition of a lobbyist
questions.stem: The disclosure statute defines a lobbyist by what the individual does for a client. Which statement describes that definition?

options.text: An individual retained for compensation whose services include more than one lobbying contact, unless lobbying takes under a fifth of the time worked for that client over three months
Any person who has ever spoken to a member of the national legislature about any subject whatever
options.misconception: believes a single conversation makes someone a lobbyist

options.text: Any individual on the payroll of a lobbying firm, however small a share the work occupies
options.misconception: believes employment by a firm alone settles the status

options.text: Any individual who is paid a fixed salary by a client, because the method of pay is what counts
options.misconception: believes the form of payment decides the status

questions.explanation: The statutory test has two parts, and a person satisfies it by doing more than one lobbying contact for a client for compensation, unless the lobbying occupies less than a fifth of the time the individual works for that client across a three-month period. The time test exists so that a general adviser who spends a small fraction of a week on legislative matters is not treated as a lobbyist, while someone whose work is mostly legislative matters is. A single contact is not enough, employment by a firm is not enough without more, and nothing in the definition turns on whether the individual is paid a salary or a fee.
questions.hint: Ask how many contacts are required, and what share of the person's time is relevant.

questions.topic: The efforts that support a lobbying contact
questions.learningObjective: state which preparatory activities the disclosure statute brings within the definition
questions.stem: The disclosure statute reaches the efforts that support a lobbying contact as well as the contact itself. Which of the following does the statute name among those efforts?

options.text: Preparation and planning, and the research and background work intended at the time for use in contacts
Only the contact itself, leaving every earlier hour of preparation outside the reporting net entirely
options.misconception: believes only the communication itself is covered

options.text: Any internal discussion among a client's own staff, whether or not a contact is ever contemplated
options.misconception: believes all internal staff work is covered

options.text: Only preparation that already appears in a printed document shown to the official beforehand
options.misconception: believes a written record is a precondition for coverage

questions.explanation: Lobbying activities are defined to include lobbying contacts and the efforts made in support of them, and the statute names preparation and planning, research and other background work intended at the time of doing it for use in contacts, and coordination with the lobbying activities of others. The qualifier about intent at the time matters, because it distinguishes work done to support a contact from work that happens to be done by the same person for another purpose. A client's internal discussion with no contact in view is not the same thing, and no written record is required before the work counts.
questions.hint: Ask what the preparatory work must be intended for, and when that intention is tested.

questions.topic: The income figure that exempts a registrant
questions.learningObjective: apply the statutory income exemption for a lobbying firm
questions.stem: A lobbying firm expects income of $2,000 in the current quarter from matters related to lobbying on behalf of one particular client. What follows under the disclosure statute?

options.text: No registration is required for that client, because the exemption is set above two thousand five hundred dollars for the quarter
Registration is required, because any income at all from a client's lobbying matters crosses the threshold
options.misconception: believes a threshold of zero triggers the registration duty

options.text: Registration is required, because the exemption reaches only an organisation's expenses and never a firm's income
options.misconception: believes the exemption is limited to organisations and not firms

options.text: No registration is required for any client at all, because the exemption is measured per firm rather than per client
options.misconception: believes the exemption is not client-specific

questions.explanation: The statute excuses a person or entity whose income from a client's matters related to lobbying does not exceed and is not expected to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars in the quarterly period in which the registration would be made, and two thousand dollars is below that figure, so the duty does not arise for that client. The figure is set per client rather than per firm, which is why the statute also requires a separate registration for each client, so an exemption for one client leaves the others untouched. A second, larger figure applies to an organisation lobbying on its own behalf, and the dollar amounts are adjusted periodically in the way the statute directs.
questions.hint: Compare the figure with the statutory figure, and check whether the test is per client or per firm.

questions.topic: When a registrant must register
questions.learningObjective: state the deadline the disclosure statute sets for a first registration
questions.stem: A person is retained by a client and makes a first lobbying contact on the same day. Under the disclosure statute, registration is due no later than when?

options.text: Forty-five days after the first contact, or the first business day after the forty-fifth if it is not one
Ten days after the first contact, so that a filing precedes anything the contact may bring about
options.misconception: believes the window is much shorter than the statute sets

options.text: Ninety days after the first contact, because a registrant may use a full quarter to file
options.misconception: believes the first return and the registration are one and the same

options.text: Only when the first quarterly report falls due, since registration follows the reporting cycle
options.misconception: believes registration and quarterly reporting are the same duty

questions.explanation: The clock runs from the earlier of two events, the first lobbying contact and the employment or retention that makes the contacts someone's work, and the deadline is forty-five days from that point, with a slip to the next business day where the forty-fifth is not one. Running the clock from whichever comes first prevents a registrant from delaying the filing by waiting for a contact after being retained. Registration is a separate duty from the quarterly reports that follow, and the ninety-day figure in the third option belongs to no deadline in the statute.
questions.hint: Find the deadline in the statute and note which of two starting points the clock runs from.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The honest-broker account of organised interests
questions.learningObjective: identify the account that treats organised interests as intermediaries
questions.stem: One influential account holds that organised interests are intermediaries who shape their demands to what the political system can actually deliver. What is that account called, and what does it assume?

options.text: The honest-broker account, which assumes groups moderate their demands because fewer demands are more likely to be met
The pluralist account, which assumes many groups competing freely cancel one another's influence out
options.misconception: believes the moderating account is the many-groups account

options.text: The three-cornered account, which assumes one committee, one agency, and one industry control a subject together
options.misconception: believes the moderating account is the closed-triangle one

options.text: The class account, which assumes one economic class decides outcomes through its own preferences
options.misconception: believes the moderating account is the class account

questions.explanation: The honest-broker account treats organised interests as intermediaries between members and government rather than as claimants whose demands must all be met, and the moderating assumption follows from the mechanism it describes: a group that puts many items on the table risks losing all of them, so it concentrates on the few it can win. That is a claim about strategy under constraint, not a claim that groups are disinterested, because a broker still serves the members who pay it. The three other accounts named here are different arguments about how influence is distributed, and none of them explains a group's moderation in these terms.
questions.hint: Ask what the account predicts a group will do when it cannot win everything it wants.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: explain why diffuse-benefit groups are harder to organise than concentrated-benefit groups
questions.stem: Why is it said that a group whose members share a small, concentrated benefit tends to organise, while a group seeking a large benefit spread thinly across many people tends not to?

options.text: Because with a thin spread each member can gain from the group's success without paying anything towards it
Because concentrated groups simply hold more money and can therefore afford a larger organisation
options.misconception: believes the explanation is only about money

options.text: Because a thin-spread group is barred by a constitutional limit that concentrated groups manage to avoid
options.misconception: believes a legal prohibition explains the difference

options.text: Because members of a thin-spread group always disagree among themselves, so no organisation can form at all
options.misconception: believes disagreement rather than incentive is the cause

questions.explanation: The difficulty is an incentive problem rather than a shortage of money or law: when a benefit is spread thinly, any single member gains a little whether or not he contributes, so the rational move is to let others pay, and if everyone reasons the same way nobody pays. Where the benefit is concentrated, the members who receive it gain enough from a successful effort that each will spend something to make it happen. The result is a durable asymmetry in the system, and it explains why groups with concentrated interests often appear to be the most assertive even when the number of people affected is small.
questions.hint: Ask what a single member loses by declining to contribute when the benefit is spread wide.

questions.topic: Clienteliage and the exchange of help for loyalty
questions.learningObjective: identify a clientelist exchange and distinguish it from a district appropriation
questions.stem: A local party worker visits households, promises a neighbour help in obtaining a permit, and secures the neighbour's loyalty in return. What is that arrangement called?

options.text: Clienteliage, in which help is delivered in exchange for a political commitment by the person helped
A district appropriation, in which national money is spent on a constituency the party holds
options.misconception: believes a benefit to a person is the same as a benefit to a district

options.text: A party discipline count, which measures how many members will support a measure the party needs
options.misconception: believes a measure of party discipline is a benefit-delivery scheme

options.text: A single-member district, which elects one representative by the largest share of votes cast
options.misconception: believes an electoral method is a benefit-delivery scheme

questions.explanation: Clienteliage is an exchange in which an individual is given assistance, often in obtaining something a government office controls, in return for political support, and it works at the level of the person rather than the district. A district appropriation spends public money on a constituency without asking any individual for anything, and while it is sometimes traded for political support, the defining feature of clienteliage is the direct and personal bargain. A party discipline count is a measure of internal party strength and a single-member district is a way of electing, and neither delivers anything to a neighbour.
questions.hint: Ask whether the benefit goes to a person who gives something in return, or to a district as a whole.

questions.topic: The pluralism and elitist disagreement
questions.learningObjective: state the two positions in the long-running argument about who decides
questions.stem: Two long-running arguments disagree about who actually gets what decided in this system. What does the pluralist account claim, and what does the elitist account claim in reply?

options.text: That many groups compete and none dominates, against the view that a much narrower set of actors has the practical say
That no group influences anything at all, against the view that business interests decide every question
options.misconception: believes one of the accounts denies all influence

options.text: That one economic class decides every case, against the view that many groups each hold a small share
options.misconception: reverses the two positions named in the question

options.text: That the question was settled by a court long ago, against the view that it is left to political scientists
options.misconception: believes the disagreement is resolved in court

questions.explanation: The pluralist account is built on the observation that many groups seek influence over the same decisions and that no one of them prevails everywhere, so power is dispersed and access depends on which groups are organised and interested in a given subject. The elitist reply is that a small number of participants dominate the resources, the positions, and the access points that matter, and that the visible competition among groups conceals a settled preference underneath. Both are empirical claims about the same system, which is why the disagreement has lasted rather than being resolved, and the third option reverses the two positions named in the question.
questions.hint: Ask which side claims dispersal and which claims concentration, and keep them the right way round.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The argument that organisations drift toward leadership control
questions.learningObjective: identify the argument that large organisations come under the control of a few
questions.stem: A long-standing argument in political science holds that large organisations, whatever their formal aims, tend over time to be run by a small leadership for its own sake. Which account is that?

options.text: The iron law of oligarchy, which attributes the drift to the friction that makes participation costly
The pluralist account, which predicts that control stays widely spread among an organisation's members
options.misconception: believes the leadership-control account is the dispersed one

options.text: The class account, which predicts that one economic class ends up running every organisation
options.misconception: believes the leadership account is an account about class

options.text: The elite account, which predicts that a narrow leadership runs the state rather than the organisations
options.misconception: believes the account concerns the state and not organisations

questions.explanation: The argument is that ordinary members find participation in a large organisation slow and unrewarding, which frees the leadership to make decisions with little interference, and that the arrangement then works well enough for most purposes to become self-reinforcing. It is an account of organisations and why their formal aims drift from what they actually do, not an account about the state, which is the distinction the fourth option loses. The class account is a separate claim about the distribution of influence across a society, and the pluralist account is a claim about how many groups can be heard rather than about who runs any one of them.
questions.hint: Ask which account is about an organisation's internal life rather than about the system as a whole.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The three-cornered policy arrangement
questions.learningObjective: identify a closed three-cornered policy relationship and its function
questions.stem: Scholars describe a stable relationship in which a committee of the legislature, an executive agency, and an industry association form a closed circle around one narrow subject. Which account describes that?

options.text: An iron triangle, in which three sets of actors exchange support and information on a single policy area
An issue network, in which many interested specialists share a concern and no official controls it
options.misconception: believes the closed three-cornered case is the open-network case

options.text: A clientelist arrangement, in which a party worker delivers help in return for political loyalty
options.misconception: believes a three-cornered policy bargain is a vote-buying scheme

options.text: A rule of construction, under which an unclear penal statute is read in the defendant's favour
options.misconception: believes a policy arrangement is a rule of construction

questions.explanation: An iron triangle names a closed relationship of exactly this shape, and it works because each corner has something the others need: the committee controls the hearing and the amendment, the agency controls the rule and the enforcement, and the association supplies information, constituency, and political cover. Because the subject is narrow, the participants can be numerous in total while the decision is taken by very few, and that is what the arrangement is for. An issue network is the contrasting picture of a policy area handled by many specialists without closed control, and neither the vote-buying scheme nor the construction rule is a relationship between institutions.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three corners gets from the other two, and whether the subject is narrow.

questions.topic: Issue networks and the limits of the three-cornered account
questions.learningObjective: explain what the issue-network account adds to the iron-triangle account
questions.stem: A second body of scholarship describes some policy areas as handled by a much larger number of actors, inside and outside government, who share expertise and among whom no one dominates. What does that account add?

options.text: That a policy area can be decided by many interested specialists rather than by a closed set of three
That the three-cornered arrangement is the normal case, and the open arrangement is a rare deviation from it
options.misconception: believes the open account is a variant of the closed one

options.text: That policy areas are settled by one agency alone, with no outside group taking part in the decision at all
options.misconception: believes the account removes outside actors entirely

options.text: That the number of actors matters less than the amount of money each one is able to spend
options.misconception: believes the account is really about resources

questions.explanation: The account was developed to explain policy areas where a subject is technically complex and no one participant has a decisive claim, so the outcome emerges from negotiation among many specialists rather than from a bargain between a small circle. It adds a second possible structure rather than displacing the first, since a single subject can look different depending on how many people are competent and interested in it. It does not claim that any one agency decides alone, and money enters the picture only as one influence among many rather than as the organising fact.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of number of participants the account requires, and what happens to the outcome.

questions.topic: The argument that the institutions explain the pattern
questions.learningObjective: identify the argument that locates the cause of outcomes in the system rather than in a class
questions.stem: A critique of the claim that one economic class determines policy argues that the system's own structure, rather than the preferences of a dominant class, produces what gets decided. Which account is that?

options.text: The mobilising-bias account, which treats the institutions themselves as the source of the pattern
The pluralist account, which attributes the pattern to the number of groups that happen to exist
options.misconception: believes the structural account is the many-groups account

options.text: The class account, which attributes the pattern to the preferences of the economically dominant class
options.misconception: believes the critique is the account it is criticising

options.text: The elite account, which attributes the pattern to a narrow leadership inside the state itself
options.misconception: believes the critique is the leadership account

questions.explanation: The argument is that groups with the greatest economic weight are not always the ones that prevail, and that the explanation lies in features of the institutions that advantage whoever is already organised for political action, such as the difficulty of mobilising a large, dispersed interest against a small, concentrated one. Outcomes are therefore read as effects of the system's design rather than as the preferences of a class being carried into law, and the claim is a causal one about where the advantage comes from. The pluralist account is a separate claim about the number of groups that can be heard, and the account in the third option is the one being answered rather than the answer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the account locates the cause inside the institutions or inside the preferences of a class.

questions.topic: What the statutory merit principles require
questions.learningObjective: identify a named principle in the federal personnel statute
questions.stem: A statute sets out the principles on which federal personnel management should be based. Which of the following is one of the principles the statute names?

options.text: That employees be protected against arbitrary action, personal favouritism, and coercion for partisan purposes
That every employee be paid at the same rate regardless of the work that the employee performs
options.misconception: believes the statute requires one uniform rate

options.text: That an employee's political affiliation be weighed when judging the adequacy of that employee's work
options.misconception: believes the statute permits partisan assessment of performance

options.text: That an employee who discloses a suspected violation be moved to a different post as a matter of course
options.misconception: believes the statute requires a transfer rather than protection

questions.explanation: The statute lists nine principles, and the protection of employees against arbitrary action, personal favouritism, and coercion for partisan political purposes is one of them, joined by a separate prohibition on using official authority to interfere with an election. Equal pay for work of equal value is a different principle, which does not require a single rate but a rate that reflects the value of the work. Nothing in the list makes political affiliation a permissible ground for judging performance, and the protection of an employee who discloses wrongdoing is a protection from reprisal, not an instruction to move her.
questions.hint: Look for the principle that limits what an agency may do to an employee, not what it must pay.

questions.topic: Competitive and excepted appointments
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a competitive appointment from an excepted one
questions.stem: Federal positions fall into more than one hiring category. What is the practical difference between the competitive service and an excepted appointment?

options.text: Competitive positions are filled through an open examination process, while excepted positions are filled outside it
Competitive positions are permanent, while excepted positions are temporary in every single case
options.misconception: believes the categories differ in duration rather than in method

options.text: Competitive positions carry no protection against political pressure, while excepted ones carry all of it
options.misconception: believes the difference lies in political activity rules

options.text: Competitive positions are unpaid, while excepted positions are all paid directly by statute
options.misconception: believes the difference lies in whether the post is paid

questions.explanation: The competitive service is the body of positions that are filled by examination, with the announcement, the written test, and the register that follows from it, and it is that method rather than the post's duties that defines the category. Excepted positions are those filled outside the examination process, because the work calls for a particular expertise, because the appointment serves a confidential or policy role, or for one of the other reasons the statutes recognise. Neither category fixes the duration or the pay of a post, and the protections against political pressure do not map neatly onto the two categories, which is why the third option overstates a distinction that is not clean.
questions.hint: Ask what each category tells you about the way the person was selected.

questions.topic: Why career staff are protected from partisan removal
questions.learningObjective: explain the institutional reason for protecting career employees from partisan removal
questions.stem: Federal agencies are staffed by a small number of political appointees and a much larger body of career employees. What is the standard reason for protecting career staff from removal for partisan reasons?

options.text: So that an administration changes with the votes while the agency's knowledge and capacity carry over
So that career staff may lobby the political appointees on behalf of the people they serve
options.misconception: believes the protection serves an organised-interest function

options.text: So that career employees may hold views opposing the elected administration without any limit at all
options.misconception: believes the protection removes political accountability entirely

options.text: So that the agency avoids the cost of recruiting and training new people whenever leadership changes
options.misconception: believes the only reason is a financial saving

questions.explanation: The appointees are there to set direction and answer to the voters, while the career staff hold the expertise that lets an agency carry out what the law requires, and protecting them from removal for political reasons is what keeps the second capacity available to the next administration. Without that separation, every change of leadership would discard the accumulated knowledge of how the agency's programmes actually work, and an agency could not be trusted to administer a statute consistently over time. The protection is not a licence to disregard the elected branch, since career staff must still carry out the policies they are given, and it is not merely a way of avoiding recruitment costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the agency would lose if its expertise left with each change of administration.

That the agency evaluate the political views of each employee it hires, once every year

options.misconception: believes the continuing duty is a funding duty

questions.topic: A rule that passes the review window
questions.learningObjective: state the default outcome when the legislature does not act on a submitted rule
questions.stem: An agency submits a rule to both houses and to the Comptroller General, and the statutory review window passes with no joint resolution of disapproval. What happens to the rule?

options.text: It takes effect on the date the statute fixes, because the window closed without a disapproval
It lapses, because a rule may take effect only if the legislature affirmatively approves it
options.misconception: believes the procedure requires affirmative approval

options.text: It waits, because the Comptroller General must first certify the agency's procedural compliance
options.misconception: believes the accounting report is a gate rather than a report

options.text: It lapses, because a single report from an agency is not enough to start the window
options.misconception: believes a second submission is required

questions.explanation: The procedure is a disapproval procedure rather than an approval one, and the rule takes effect on the later of the sixty days that follow the legislature's receipt of the report or its publication, or the date the rule would otherwise have taken effect. Silence leaves the rule intact, and the statute goes further and forbids any court or agency from reading an intent about the rule into the legislature's inaction.

That government proceeds by ranking every alternative against a single overall goal before deciding

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why the disclosure statute defines its terms narrowly
questions.learningObjective: explain the design logic of the statutory definitions in the lobbying-disclosure statute
questions.stem: A disclosure statute defines a lobbying contact, a lobbying firm, a lobbyist, and the officials it covers, and then sets out a long list of communications that are not a lobbying contact. Explain why the drafters drew those lines as they did, what the definition of a lobbying contact includes as well as excludes, and what would go wrong if the statute were drawn more broadly.

answer.exemplar: The definitions are drawn narrowly because the statute imposes a filing duty and a disclosure duty on ordinary people, and a definition broad enough to catch every conversation about government would place that burden on a great many of them, most of whom are not seeking to influence anything and would simply stop participating. The line is therefore drawn around four federal subject matters, namely the formulation, modification, or adoption of federal legislation; of a federal rule, regulation, executive order, or programme, policy, or position; of the administration or execution of a federal programme, which reaches contracts, grants, loans, permits, and licences; and of a nomination or confirmation, and a lobbying contact is an oral or written communication to a defined list of officials on one of those matters on behalf of a client. Lobbying activities then sweep in the preparation, planning, research, and coordination that support such a contact, so that the statute cannot be evaded by doing the thinking somewhere other than in front of the official, while the list of exclusions takes back the communications that look similar but are not private approaches: testimony before a committee, a comment filed on the record in a public proceeding, the gathering and dissemination of news, a request for specific information, a communication by a public official in an official capacity, and a communication made on behalf of a foreign government under the separate registration regime. A broader draft would fail for the reason the narrow one is written the way it is, because a duty that cannot be avoided is a duty that will be ignored, and a person who has to file a quarterly return because they once asked for a meeting stops asking for meetings, which is a worse outcome for the transparency the statute is trying to produce.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the four federal subject matters that define a lobbying contact, explains that the statute also reaches preparation and coordination so that the work cannot be relocated, and accounts for the exclusion list as a way of keeping the duty off people who are not seeking to influence anyone. It should also give a reason for the narrowness rather than reporting it, and should say what would go wrong if the lines were drawn widely. An answer that paraphrases the definitions without reasoning about the burden they impose, or that treats the exclusion list as arbitrary housekeeping, has reported the statute rather than explained it.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: the four matters brought within the definition, the exclusions, and the reason for drawing the line there.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a career civil service is defended
questions.learningObjective: explain the problem each personnel protection addresses and the cost of the arrangement
questions.stem: The federal personnel statutes bar the removal of a career employee for partisan reasons, list practices an agency may not commit against an employee, and set out nine principles on which personnel management should rest. Explain the problem that each part addresses, why the protections were adopted, and what the arrangement costs.

answer.exemplar: Each part answers a different way in which the personnel system could be used against the person it is meant to serve. The bar on partisan removal addresses the risk that an administration would treat the service as its own, emptying the agency of experienced staff at each change of leadership and destroying the knowledge on which consistent administration of a statute depends. The list of forbidden practices addresses pressure applied inside the agency, whether the coercion of an employee for partisan purposes, the use of official authority to affect an election, or reprisal for a lawful disclosure of a violation of law, a gross waste of funds, or an abuse of authority, and the last of these is the reason a body outside the agency was created to receive such complaints. The nine principles address the ordinary condition of employment, requiring that selection rest on relative ability after fair and open competition, that treatment be fair without regard to political affiliation, that equal pay be given for work of equal value, that employees be retained on the adequacy of their performance, and that the work force be used efficiently. The reason for adopting the scheme as a whole was that a government which must re-train a workforce at every election is a government that administers its programmes badly, and the cost is real: a person who has been kept in post cannot be dismissed merely because a new leadership dislikes the department, and the remedy for a genuinely incompetent employee is correspondingly harder, which is why the statutes pair the protection with review of adverse actions by a board and with a duty to correct inadequate performance. The arrangement therefore buys competence and continuity at the price of a slower response to political failure, and the question it raises is whether the courts and the board are quick enough to supply what the protection withholds.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the three parts of the scheme and says what each is for, ties the protection from reprisal to the existence of a body that receives complaints from outside the agency, and then gives a genuine cost rather than presenting the arrangement as costless. It should note that the protection is paired with review by a board and with a duty to correct inadequate performance, since that pairing is what answers the argument that an incompetent employee can never be removed. An answer that lists the provisions as protections without naming the abuse each prevents, or that treats the merit principles as a pay rule, has not explained the design.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: the abuse each part prevents, the reason for the scheme as a whole, and the price paid for it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two reforms and the doctrines each serves
questions.learningObjective: synthesise a disclosure duty and a procedural limit into a single comparison
questions.stem: One reform would require an agency to publish, before it may act, the specific information it is asking the public to supply. A second would require a committee of the legislature to obtain an order from a court before questioning an official of the agency. Using the doctrines rather than the names of the parties, explain what each reform is designed to produce, why they are likely to produce opposite results, and what the second reform would change about the character of the relationship between the two institutions.

answer.exemplar: The two reforms are aimed at the same general problem, which is that a decision made by an institution that is not answerable to the people affected by it will not be made well, and they answer it in opposite ways. The first is a disclosure requirement of the kind the information statute supplies, directed at the demand the government makes on the public rather than at the decision itself, and it works by making the burden visible before the burden is imposed, so that a person who finds the request duplicative, unclear, or disproportionate can say so while it can still be changed. Its force is entirely in the prospect of objection, because nobody has to sue and no court is involved. The second is a procedural limit of a different kind, requiring a judicial order before a legislative committee may examine an official, and its effect is to convert a working relationship into an adversarial one: the committee would have to establish a case in a court before it could ask a question, the agency would gain a forum in which to resist, and the delay would give a subject that benefits from quiet a further advantage. A disclosure duty before action and a court order before questioning are therefore opposites in one respect and mirrors in another, since both work by putting a moment between the institution and the act, but the first moment is opened to the affected public and the second is closed to it. The second reform would also unsettle the informal channels by which oversight actually works, because much of what a committee learns comes from asking questions that produce no evidence and attract no procedure, and a rule requiring an order in advance would leave only the formal record on which the argument in the fourth option depends.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the common problem, explains that the first reform works through visibility and the prospect of objection with no litigation involved, and explains that the second works by inserting a court and a case between the committee and the agency, with the delay and the defensive posture that follows. It should also say what the second reform would do to the informal working relationship, since that is the part of the comparison the item sets. An answer that calls both reforms oversight or transparency without distinguishing the moment at which each operates, or that assumes the second would strengthen the questioning rather than change its character, has not made the comparison.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: the shared problem, why the two mechanisms differ, and what a court order would do to the relationship between the institutions.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The order of steps in a disclosure workflow
questions.learningObjective: correct a misplaced arrow in a diagram of the disclosure workflow
questions.stem: A diagram of the disclosure workflow shows three boxes joined by arrows. The boxes are: a lobbying contact is made, a registration is filed within forty-five days of the trigger, and a quarterly report of activity is published. The arrows as drawn run from the quarterly report back to the contact, and from the contact to the registration. One arrow is drawn in the wrong place. Which arrow is misplaced, and what is the correct order for the two boxes it connects?

options.text: The arrow from the report back to the contact, because the contact is the event that starts the clock
The arrow from the contact to the registration, because a report is filed before any contact is made
options.misconception: believes a report precedes the first contact

options.text: The arrow from the report back to the contact, because the report is the event that starts the clock
options.misconception: believes the reporting cycle starts the registration clock

options.text: The arrow from the contact to the registration, because a registration is filed only after the first report
options.misconception: believes registration follows the first report

questions.explanation: The workflow runs forward, and the event that starts it is the one the statute names as the trigger for the filing deadline, which is a lobbying contact, or the retention that makes such contacts someone's work, whichever occurs first. The registration follows inside forty-five days, and the quarterly report of activity is a later and continuing duty that describes what has been done since, so an arrow running from the report back to the contact reverses the direction of time. The arrow from the contact to the registration is in the right order, which is why the second and fourth options, both of which condemn the correct arrow, are wrong.
questions.hint: Ask which event the statute treats as starting the clock, and which of the two arrows runs against the order of events.
